prescriptions.title: Prescription · Amoxicillin course
prescriptions.summary: Short antibiotic course for a bacterial infection with symptomatic fever relief.

medicines.name: Amoxicillin
medicines.dosageLine: 1 capsule · 3 times a day · 7 days · After food

medicines.name: Paracetamol
medicines.dosageLine: 1 tablet · up to 3 times a day · For fever

riskAnalysis: No major drug-drug interactions detected between the prescribed medicines.
Amoxicillin: do NOT take if there is a known penicillin allergy.
insights: Complete the full 7-day antibiotic course even if you feel better.
Take Amoxicillin with food to reduce stomach upset.
Stop and seek care immediately if you notice rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing.

prescriptions.title: Prescription · Diabetes management
prescriptions.summary: Type 2 diabetes management with combined oral hypoglycaemic agents.

medicines.name: Metformin
medicines.dosageLine: 1 tablet · 2 times a day · With meals

medicines.name: Glimepiride
medicines.riskNote: Risk of low blood sugar - watch for dizziness, sweating or confusion.

riskAnalysis: Glimepiride + Metformin together increase the risk of hypoglycaemia - monitor blood glucose.
Avoid alcohol; it can amplify low blood-sugar episodes.
insights: Check fasting blood sugar regularly and log the readings.
Carry a fast-acting sugar source (glucose / juice) for hypoglycaemia.
Pair medication with a consistent diet and light daily exercise.

prescriptions.title: Prescription · Hypertension
prescriptions.summary: Blood-pressure control with a calcium-channel blocker and a beta-blocker.

medicines.name: Atenolol
medicines.riskNote: May lower heart rate - report unusual fatigue or fainting.

riskAnalysis: Combined antihypertensives cause additive blood-pressure lowering - rise slowly from sitting/lying.
Amlodipine can cause ankle swelling - monitor and report if marked.
insights: Take both medicines at the same time each day.
Reduce dietary salt and processed foods.
Measure blood pressure at home at least twice a week.

prescriptions.title: Prescription · Hypothyroidism

medicines.name: Levothyroxine
medicines.dosageLine: 1 tablet · once daily · Empty stomach, morning

riskAnalysis: Take on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast for proper absorption.
Separate from calcium or iron supplements by at least 4 hours.
insights: Do not skip doses - thyroid levels need a steady supply.
Re-test TSH in 6-8 weeks and adjust dose with your doctor.
Tell your doctor about any new supplements or medicines.

prescriptions.title: Prescription · Cardiac / cholesterol
prescriptions.summary: Secondary cardiac prevention with a statin and low-dose aspirin.

medicines.name: Aspirin
medicines.riskNote: Increased bleeding risk - report black stools or easy bruising.

riskAnalysis: Statin + aspirin is common in cardiac care, but watch for muscle pain and bleeding.
Report unexplained muscle aches or weakness (possible statin myopathy).
insights: Take the statin at night for best cholesterol-lowering effect.
Avoid grapefruit juice while on atorvastatin.
Get a fasting lipid panel in 8-12 weeks.

prescriptions.title: Lab Panel · Lipid, CBC & Thyroid (05 Feb 2026)
prescriptions.summary: Fasting lipid profile, complete blood count with ESR, and thyroid panel for a 58-year-old woman. Most results are within normal limits. Two findings stand out and warrant a doctor's review: the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is clearly raised at 9.34 (normal 0.54–5.3) while FT3 and FT4 are normal — a pattern consistent with subclinical hypothyroidism — and serum uric acid is high at 7.0 (normal 2.4–5.7). Cholesterol is well controlled overall, with LDL only mildly above the optimal target.
riskAnalysis: TSH high at 9.34 µIU/mL (ref 0.54–5.3) with normal FT3 (2.41) and FT4 (1.15) — pattern of subclinical hypothyroidism; an underactive thyroid that may need monitoring or treatment.
Uric Acid high at 7.0 mg/dL (ref 2.4–5.7) — hyperuricemia, which raises the risk of gout and kidney stones.
LDL Cholesterol 119 mg/dL (optimal <100) and Non-HDL 145.6 mg/dL (optimal <130) are mildly above optimal targets.
MCHC slightly low at 30.9 gm/dL (ref 31.5–34.5) and absolute monocytes slightly low at 187 cells/cu.mm (ref 200–1000) — minor, generally not significant in isolation.
ESR is at the upper end of normal (18 mm/hr, ref 5–20); blood count is otherwise unremarkable with normal haemoglobin and platelets.
insights: Share this report with your doctor — the raised TSH most likely needs a repeat thyroid test and a clinical review to decide if treatment is required.
The high uric acid can often be helped by staying well hydrated and reducing red meat, organ meats, shellfish, alcohol and sugary drinks; your doctor may check kidney function.
Lipids are largely well controlled; keeping up a heart-healthy diet and regular activity should help bring LDL fully into the optimal range.
Overall blood count is reassuring — normal haemoglobin, white cells and platelets, with no sign of anaemia or infection.
This is informational only and not a diagnosis; please confirm all findings and next steps with your physician.
